job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up late-ish, around nine, and sit at the kitchen table at my parents' flat in Coventry with a cold tea and the job boards. I graduated in mechanical engineering in the summer, a plain pass, and my final project was a test rig for a small gearbox. I send maybe three applications a day and get mostly automatic rejections. Afternoons I help my dad, who runs a pharmacy, with deliveries just to feel useful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work itself, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum says the right job will come and she isn't pushing me. That helps, but it also makes me feel like I'm being patient with myself for no reason. I haven't done any internships, and every posting asks for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've thought all along: a lot of noise from tech companies selling software. At home I'd say good, nothing breaks. I wouldn't post about it, because I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be stuck with the same problem, which is no offer and no internship on my CV. Plateau doesn't fix that. I do have savings and my parents, so I'm not scared, just stuck and a bit embarrassed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aim for 15 applications a week to manufacturing firms around Coventry, and ask my old project supervisor, Dr Okafor, for a reference. I'd also ring two firms that never answered. I still wouldn't touch any AI tool, because I don't trust what it writes about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, mostly. It's not frightening, it's just a long wait. Some days I feel fine and some days I feel like everyone else got the memo and I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust AI tools. What happened to make you feel that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In second year a classmate used an AI tool for a stress calculation and it gave a confident wrong number. Our tutor caught it. I'd rather be slow and right than let a tool put a confident wrong number next to my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the job hunt feels most unfair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That firms want two years of experience for an entry-level role. I wish the big firms had to run proper apprenticeships, with a rule on it. Otherwise they just let people like me sit at kitchen tables.

say: I'd tell friends **nothing changes** and the hype was a sales trick.
Online I'd stay quiet, because I don't post my opinions.
think: The **missing internship** is my real problem, and AI has nothing to do with it.
I'm not scared of money trouble, but I'm **stuck** and embarrassed.
do: Send **15 applications a week** to manufacturers around Coventry.
Ask Dr Okafor (my project supervisor) for a **reference** and chase two silent firms by phone.
feel: **Flat** and impatient, a long wait with no end date.
S0.quote: I'd rather be slow and right than let a tool put a confident wrong number next to my name.
fieldNote: Distrust of **AI** comes from a specific classroom moment, not from ideology.
Her worry is the **job gap**, and a safe cushion keeps her from panic.
Reaches for **rules** on employers, in line with progressive views.

steps.text: Send 15 applications a week to Coventry manufacturers
Wait for replies from two firms before widening the search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions should be preparing for. Entry-level work is the first thing firms will hand to software, because it's the cheap part of any job. I'd say it loudly at the family table, where my uncle thinks I'm being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the grad roles I'm applying for are the very ones that shrink. Drawing checks, report writing, spec sheets, a lot of that is thinking work. Mechanical jobs on a factory floor last longer, but those are the ones I'm told need experience first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the search to maintenance and test engineering, which are more hands-on, and apply to two apprenticeship schemes even though they pay less. I'd also join the engineers' professional body so I'm at least in a room with people. I still wouldn't use AI, but I might sit through one workshop so I know what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can pay my own way for a good while, so it's not panic. But I can see the door narrowing while I stand outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit through a workshop. What would change your mind about using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a person I trust get a good result and still be responsible for it. If a firm has a rule that says who checks the output, I'd feel safer. Right now it looks like nobody is in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for entry-level jobs shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that cut training budgets, and the government that lets them. Nobody forced companies to stop hiring juniors, they just found it cheaper. That's a choice, not weather.

say: I'd tell family that **entry-level jobs** are the first to go and unions should plan for it.
I'd call for rules making firms keep training juniors.
think: The graduate roles I'm applying for are the ones **most likely to shrink**.
Hands-on engineering lasts longer, but wants **experience** I don't have.
do: Apply to **maintenance and test engineering** roles, and two apprenticeship schemes that pay less.
Join the engineers' **professional body** to get into rooms with working people.
feel: **Anxious**: money is fine, but the door looks like it's narrowing.
S1.quote: Nobody forced companies to stop hiring juniors, they just found it cheaper. That's a choice, not weather.
fieldNote: Blames **employers and government** rather than the technology.
Willing to bend on **pay** and and role type, but not on tool use.
Notable that her **condition** for for using AI is clear human responsibility.

steps.text: Apply to maintenance and test engineering roles around Coventry
Join the engineers' professional body and go to its local meetings
Attend one free workshop on AI tools in engineering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless. Two years is nothing, and nobody has asked ordinary people if they agree. I'd go on any march that was organised, and I'd sign anything asking for rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it frightens me. I'm 23 with a pass degree and no experience, and two years from now the entry-level jobs I wanted may be handled by software. Robots for the factory work come three years after that, so I'd have a short gap. My cushion helps, but a cushion only lasts so long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop being picky and take any engineering job offered, even a poor one, so I'm inside a company. I'd tell my dad I might need to work at the pharmacy full-time for a while, and I'd put my savings in a plain account and not touch them. I'd also finally learn the AI tools, grudgingly, because refusing seems pointless if everyone else has them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I lie awake doing sums on how long my savings last if there's no entry route at all. The thing I hate most is that I'd have no say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finally learn the tools. How does that sit with how you feel about them now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. It feels like surrendering. But I'd rather be the person who knows how AI fails than the one it replaces. I'd keep a notebook of every mistake it makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not going to disappear, I'll work at the pharmacy counter if I must. I'd also ask whether we can stop pretending the right job is coming. She'd cry a bit, I think.

say: I'd call it **reckless** and join any organised march for rules.
I'd sign petitions asking for a say over how fast it comes.
think: With a pass degree and **no experience**, I could be shut out of my own field.
My savings are a **cushion**, but not forever.
do: Take **any engineering job** offered so I'm inside a company.
Keep savings in a **plain account** and help full-time at my dad's pharmacy if needed.
feel: **Alarmed**: I'd lie awake counting how long savings last.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the person who knows how AI fails than the one it replaces.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to AI cracks under pressure but stays emotional.
Fear is about being **shut out**, not hunger; the cushion buys **time** only.
Has a clear **fallback** in the family pharmacy.

steps.text: Accept the first engineering job offer, even a poor one
Move savings into a plain account and leave it alone
Learn one AI tool and log every mistake it makes
Join organised marches calling for rules on AI speed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to act if governments actually bother. I'd push for rules on what firms can hand over to AI and for guaranteed training places. I'd say it at the family dinner and at any local meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's more manageable. Five years is enough to get a first job, build experience and be a person with something to lose, which weirdly helps. By 2031 I could be a junior engineer with some years behind me, if I get going now. Robots for the physical side come a few years later, so my kind of work holds longer than coding does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent job within six months, then use the evenings to get a chartered-engineer pathway going. I'd keep half my savings for a flat deposit and not spend it. I'd try the AI tools in small, low-risk ways, like checking my own spreadsheets, never for design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, a bit determined. Five years makes me feel I have a window and shouldn't waste it, and that's pressure I already feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned guaranteed training places. Who should pay for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms, through a levy. If big firms take the benefit of AI, they should pay a levy for training juniors, because they caused the cut. I'd rather that than the taxpayer funding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan. In the two-year picture I'd panic and grab anything. Here I'd choose a job in a firm that lets juniors see the whole project, not one that just puts them on a screen.

say: I'd push for a **training levy** on firms that hand work to AI.
I'd say five years is enough time if governments act.
think: This is **manageable**: five years lets me get a job and build a record.
Hands-on engineering should hold longer than **screen work**.
do: Take the first decent job within **six months**.
Keep half my savings for a **flat deposit** and use evenings for chartership.
feel: **Anxious but determined**: a window exists and I mustn't waste it.
S3.quote: If big firms take the benefit of AI, they should pay a levy for training juniors, because they caused the cut.
fieldNote: Moves from **panic** to to planning when time is longer.
Specific **policy idea**: a levy on firms, which is typical of progressive outlook.
Wants a firm that shows **juniors** the shows juniors the whole project.

steps.text: Take the first decent engineering job within six months
Keep half my savings aside for a flat deposit
Back a training levy at local political meetings
Start the chartered engineer pathway in evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like a long time, so I'd probably say it's something to prepare for, not panic about. I'd tell friends to keep an eye on policy and be ready. At home, honestly, I'd say it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it feels almost kind. A decade is enough to get a first job, get promoted, maybe be a project engineer by 2036. If things go the way I hope, I'd have a career before the robots even reach a hands-on trade like mine. My worry is that nobody uses the decade well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the ordinary job hunt, and aim for a firm that does real hardware work. Then I'd study part-time for a master's in something harder for AI to copy, like systems safety and standards. I'd also join the union branch at work. And I'd save a fixed amount each month, since I have the room to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but uneasy underneath. I'd feel in control, though the first job still isn't solved in this picture, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger cousin who's starting an engineering degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do an internship every summer, even if it's unpaid, and get a mentor. And don't ignore AI like I did. Learn it early and keep a firm line on what you check by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody uses the decade well. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments and employers will say there's time, then do nothing until year nine. I'd want a person in power to name what happens to juniors by name, not just say 'transition'.

say: I'd tell friends to **prepare**, not panic, and to follow policy.
At home I'd say it feels far off.
think: A decade is enough for a **real career** before robots reach hands-on engineering.
My worry is **nobody uses** the decade well, including me.
do: Land a first job at a firm doing **real hardware work**.
Study part-time for a master's in **systems safety**, and save a set sum monthly.
feel: **Uneasy** underneath: I'm in control, but the first job still isn't solved.
S4.quote: Governments and employers will say there's time, then do nothing until year nine.
fieldNote: **Longer horizon** softens her tone but not her distrust of institutions.
Her advice to a cousin shows she **regrets** skipping shows she regrets skipping internships and AI.
Plans a **part-time master's** in master's in a field she expects to hold up.

steps.text: Land a first job at a firm doing real hardware work
Start a part-time master's in systems safety and standards
Save a fixed sum each month from the first pay cheque
Join the union branch at my first workplace

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years worries me most. Everything I'd do depends on having time, and two years gives none. What would help is a firm rule that companies keep taking junior engineers, plus a real training place, not just a posting that asks for experience.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say one thing. People like me aren't lazy. I applied to over 200 jobs this year. I wish journalists would say that when they write about my age group.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't lazy. I applied to over 200 jobs this year.
portrait: Vera is **23**, a mechanical engineering graduate with a plain pass, living with her parents in Coventry and applying for work.
She **avoids AI tools** after seeing a confident wrong answer in a stress calculation, and only softens when pressed.
She is progressive, blames **employers and government** for cutting junior training, and would back levies, unions and rules.
Her cushion keeps her from panic, so her mood moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** only with the 2028 date.
With ten years she plans a part-time master's and a steady career, but expects institutions to waste the time.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because there would be no time to find a first job and learn the tools.
whatWouldHelp: A **firm rule** that companies keep hiring and training junior engineers, plus real training places that don't demand experience first.
